title: Imperfect review: pouvais, voulais, étais, avais
subtitle: Talking about past states and situations
explanation: Course 7 reviews common imperfect forms for things you could do, wanted, were, or had in the past. The negative goes around the verb with ne ... pas.

examples.fre: Je ne pouvais pas aller l'année dernière.

examples.eng: I wanted to go to Cape Verde.
I couldn't go last year because I had no money
examples.fre: Je ne pouvais pas aller l'année dernière parce que je n'avais pas d'argent

title: Inversion with tu / vous
subtitle: Asking direct questions
explanation: Swap the verb and subject pronoun to form a direct question. Course 7 practises this with tu and vous, especially with venir.

examples.eng: Are you coming to the beach?
examples.fre: Viens-tu à la plage? / Venez-vous à la plage?

examples.eng: Where do you come from? (formal / plural)

title: Negative inversion
subtitle: Asking negative questions
explanation: Put ne before the inverted verb and pas after the subject to ask a negative question such as 'aren’t you coming?'.

examples.fre: Ne viens-tu pas demain? / Ne venez-vous pas demain?

examples.eng: Why don't you come to France?
examples.fre: Pourquoi ne viens-tu pas en France? / Pourquoi ne venez-vous pas en France?
Ne viens-tu pas de Paris? / Ne venez-vous pas de Paris?

title: Venir de
subtitle: Saying where someone comes from
explanation: Use venir de to say where someone comes from. The form after de changes naturally with the place that follows.

title: À l'étranger / de l'étranger
subtitle: Talking about abroad
explanation: Use à l'étranger for going or being abroad, and de l'étranger for coming from abroad.

examples.eng: Why don't you come abroad with me?
examples.fre: Pourquoi ne viens-tu pas à l'étranger avec moi? / Pourquoi ne venez-vous pas à l'étranger avec moi?

title: Parler + language
subtitle: Saying which languages you speak
explanation: Use parler directly before a language name: parler français, parler anglais, and so on. In a question, the verb can come before the subject pronoun.

title: Passer + time
subtitle: Spending time or holidays
explanation: Use passer to talk about spending time somewhere. It can be used for holidays, days, weeks, or other periods of time.

examples.eng: I want to spend the holidays here.
examples.fre: Je veux passer les vacances ici.

examples.eng: I'm going to spend the holidays at the beach.
examples.fre: Je vais passer les vacances à la plage.

examples.eng: Where did you spend the holidays?
examples.fre: Où as-tu passé les vacances? / Où avez-vous passé les vacances?

title: À / en / au / aux with places
subtitle: Going to cities and countries
explanation: French uses different forms before places. Course 7 shows à with cities, en with many countries, au with masculine countries, and aux with plural countries.

examples.eng: I'm going to the United States (p/ura/)

title: Aimer + noun or infinitive
subtitle: Saying what you like
explanation: Use aimer before a noun to say you like a thing, or before an infinitive to say you like doing something. Use ne ... pas to say you do not like it.

examples.eng: I like Speaking French (literally: I like to speak French)
I don't like the food here.
examples.fre: Je n'aime pas la nourriture ici.

title: Passé composé with aller
subtitle: Saying where you went
explanation: In these Course 7 examples, aller uses être in the passé composé: je suis allé. Add a place or time expression after it.

title: Il y a + time
subtitle: Saying “ago”
explanation: Put il y a before a length of time to say how long ago something happened.

examples.eng: I went to London three days ago.
examples.fre: Je suis allé à Londres il y a trois jours.

examples.eng: We ate here two weeks ago.
examples.fre: Nous avons mangé ici il y a deux semaines.

title: Dernier / cette / prochain
subtitle: Last, this, and next
explanation: Course 7 uses dernier, cette, and prochain to place events in time. Notice that the French word order changes depending on the expression.

title: Habiter + place
subtitle: Saying where you live
explanation: Use habiter with the same place patterns seen elsewhere: à with a city, en with many countries, and au with masculine countries.

title: Depuis
subtitle: An action continuing until now
explanation: Use depuis with an action or situation that started in the past and is still true now. French often keeps the present tense where English uses 'have been'.

examples.eng: I've been living here for three months ( I live here since three months)
I've been here for two hours.
examples.fre: Je suis ici depuis deux heures.

examples.eng: I've been living here in Paris for two months.
examples.fre: J'habite ici à Paris depuis deux mois.

title: Depuis quand
subtitle: Asking “how long?”
explanation: Use depuis quand to ask when an ongoing situation started. It literally means 'since when'.

examples.eng: How long have you been living here? (Since when do you live here?)
How long have you been living in France? (Since when do you live in France?)
How long have you been living abroad?
examples.fre: Depuis quand habites-tu à l'étranger? / Depuis quand habitez-vous à l'étranger?

title: Jusqu'à / jusqu'au
subtitle: Saying “until”
explanation: Use jusqu'à to mark the end point of a period. It combines with the expression that follows, such as jusqu'à la semaine prochaine or jusqu'au mois prochain.

examples.eng: I am here until next week.
examples.fre: Je suis ici jusqu'à la semaine prochaine.
Je suis ici jusqu'au mois prochain
Je suis ici jusqu'à ce soir.

title: Days: dernier, prochain, tous les
subtitle: Last, next, and every day
explanation: With weekdays, dernier and prochain can mean last and next. Tous les + plural weekday is used for a repeated day such as every Friday.

examples.fre: Vous voyez Marie tous les vendredis.

title: Est-ce que c'est... ?
subtitle: Asking “is it...?”
explanation: Use est-ce que c'est to ask a clear yes/no question about something.

title: C'était / ce n'était pas
subtitle: Talking about what something was
explanation: Use c'était for 'it was' and ce n'était pas for 'it wasn't'. Course 7 also uses est-ce que to turn these into questions.

examples.fre: Est-ce que ce n'était pas très bon?

title: Assez
subtitle: Quite or enough
explanation: Assez can mean 'quite' before an adjective, or 'enough' when talking about an amount. With a noun, Course 7 shows assez de.

examples.eng: it is quite good / it is rather good

examples.fre: il y a assez de nourriture

title: Devant / derrière
subtitle: In front of and behind
explanation: Use devant for 'in front of' and derrière for 'behind'. They can be followed by a noun or a person.

examples.eng: It's in front of the restaurant.

title: À côté de
subtitle: Saying “next to”
explanation: Use à côté de for 'next to'. Before le and les, de combines to make du and des.

examples.eng: The cinema is next to the hotel.
examples.fre: Le cinéma est à côté de l'hôtel.

examples.eng: The toilets are next to the bar
examples.fre: Les toilettes sont à côté du bar

title: À + distance + de
subtitle: Saying how far away something is
explanation: Use être or habiter + à + distance + de to say how far a place or person is from another point.

examples.eng: I live 5 kilometres from the Eiffel Tower.
examples.fre: J'habite à cinq kilomètres de la Tour Eiffel.

examples.eng: It's thirty kilometres from the hotel
examples.fre: C'est à trente kilomètres de l'hôtel

title: En + transport / à pied
subtitle: Saying how you travel
explanation: Use en with many vehicles, such as en car or en train. Use à pied for travelling on foot.

examples.eng: I'm going there on the train tomorrow.
examples.fre: Je vais là en train demain.

title: Le trajet dure
subtitle: Saying how long a journey takes
explanation: Use le trajet dure + time to say how long a journey lasts or takes.

examples.eng: The journey takes an hour by coach
examples.fre: Le trajet dure une heure en car

examples.eng: The journey takes five hours by boat
examples.fre: Le trajet dure cinq heures en bateau

title: Present tense with vous
subtitle: Talking to one person formally or several people
explanation: Course 7 practises many present-tense verbs with vous. The verb ending changes, but vous stays before the verb in a normal statement.

examples.eng: You have a lot of food.

title: Vous + ne ... pas
subtitle: Making present-tense negatives
explanation: Put ne before the vous-form verb and pas after it to make a negative statement.

examples.eng: you don't eat / you're not eating

title: Vous inversion questions
subtitle: Turning vous statements into questions
explanation: Put the verb before vous and join them with a hyphen to form a direct question.

examples.eng: Do you speak French? / Are you speaking French?
Where are you staying this week?
Do you eat meat? (you eat meat?)

title: Negative questions with vous
subtitle: Asking “don’t you...?”
explanation: For a negative inversion question, put ne before the verb and pas after vous: ne + verb-vous + pas.

examples.eng: Don't you eat? / aren't you eating?
Why aren't you going on holiday this year?
examples.fre: Pourquoi n'allez-vous pas en vacances cette année?

examples.eng: Why don't you do that tomorrow?
examples.fre: Pourquoi ne faites-vous pas cela demain?

title: Vous imperative
subtitle: Giving instructions and commands
explanation: Use the vous verb form without the subject pronoun to give a polite or plural command.

examples.fre: Essayez ce gâteau; il est délicieux!

title: Negative vous imperative
subtitle: Telling someone not to do something
explanation: Put ne ... pas around the command form to tell someone not to do something.

examples.eng: Don't buy the food until Friday.
examples.fre: N'achetez pas la nourriture jusqu'à vendredi.

examples.eng: Don't eat too much; we're going to the restaurant later
examples.fre: Ne mangez pas trop; nous allons au restaurant plus tard
